data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism invokes an external justification while simultaneously denying that any deeper ground exists — triggering its own defeating countercondition. The mechanism states the preference is 'defensible because without it, the game of science... stops' and rests on 'the desire to play the game.' This is an instrumental justification: the rule is justified by the external criterion that science must continue. Yet the target's own countercondition explicitly flags 'If a constitutive rule must itself be justified by external criteria to be rational' as a scenario that defeats its position. By defending the preference via the instrumental value of keeping inquiry going (avoiding the cessation of science), the target appeals to exactly the kind of external criterion its countercondition says would undermine it. The claim that the commitment rests on 'no deeper logical ground than the desire to play the game' is self-undermining: the desire to play is itself a normative criterion external to the constitutive rule, and invoking it as the basis for defensibility concedes that the rule is not rationally self-grounding but requires an external justification the target cannot coherently endorse.
